lesson.title: Nature's Specialists: Enzyme Catalysis
lesson.summary: Enzymes are biological catalysts, almost always proteins, that speed up specific reactions by binding reactant molecules called substrates at a precisely shaped active site and providing a dramatically lower activation energy pathway.
lesson.body:
An enzyme is a catalyst produced by a living organism, and the overwhelming majority of enzymes are proteins, though a small number of RNA based catalysts, called ribozymes, also exist. What sets enzymes apart from most other catalysts is their specificity: a given enzyme typically catalyzes one particular reaction, or a narrow class of closely related reactions, and essentially nothing else. That specificity comes from the enzyme's active site, a pocket on the protein's surface built from a particular arrangement of amino acid side chains, whose shape and chemical environment fit the intended reactant, called the substrate, closely. The classic description of this fit is the lock and key model, though a more accurate modern picture is induced fit, in which the active site flexes slightly as the substrate binds, molding itself around the substrate rather than being a perfectly rigid shape from the start.

Catalase offers a direct, concrete comparison to the catalysis already discussed. It catalyzes exactly the same reaction as the manganese dioxide example from the catalysis chapter, the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, 2H2O2 forming 2H2O plus O2. Catalase is found in the liver and in nearly all living cells, where it is essential because hydrogen peroxide is generated as a toxic byproduct of normal metabolism and needs to be broken down quickly before it can damage DNA and proteins. Catalase does this job extremely fast, ranking among the most efficient enzymes known, with a single catalase molecule capable of processing on the order of millions of hydrogen peroxide molecules every second. The comparison is instructive: the exact same overall reaction can be catalyzed by an inorganic solid surface, manganese dioxide, working heterogeneously, or by a biological protein, catalase, working through a precisely shaped active site, and both achieve the same fundamental result, a lower activation energy pathway from reactants to products.

The specificity difference between the two is worth dwelling on. Manganese dioxide will catalyze the decomposition of essentially any hydrogen peroxide molecule that reaches its surface, and it has no particular selectivity beyond that. Catalase's active site, by contrast, is shaped specifically to bind hydrogen peroxide and will not catalyze the breakdown of unrelated molecules. This kind of selectivity is not incidental, it is essential to how cells function, since thousands of different reactions have to proceed simultaneously inside the same cell, each one needing to run without interfering with all the others, and having a distinct, highly specific enzyme for each reaction is what makes that possible.

Digestive enzymes offer another everyday example of this same specificity. Amylase, present in saliva, specifically catalyzes the hydrolysis of starch into smaller sugars such as maltose. It has no effect on proteins or fats, which require entirely different enzymes, proteases and lipases respectively, to be broken down. Underneath all of this specificity, enzymes obey the exact same underlying principles as any other catalyst covered so far: they lower the activation energy of the reaction they catalyze, they provide an alternative pathway from reactants to products, and they are not consumed overall, being regenerated at the end of each catalytic cycle so they can bind the next substrate molecule. Enzymes are simply an extraordinarily selective, biologically evolved variety of that same general idea.
